newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SWEDEN CAN'T BAN TV CHILD ADS FROM ABROAD-EU COURT.
newsitem.headline: SWEDEN CAN'T BAN TV CHILD ADS FROM ABROAD-EU COURT.

text.p: The European Court of Justice ruled on Wednesday that Sweden, which bans TV advertising aimed at children, cannot block commercials broadcast from another European Union member state.

"A member state may penalise an advertiser on account of misleading advertising coming from another member state but may not do so simply on the ground that the advertising is directed at children," the Luxembourg-based EU court said in a statement.
But there was nothing in the EU's Television without Frontiers law to prevent Stockholm from applying stricter rules for broadcasters based in Sweden.
"This consideration cannot apply to television broadcasters established in other member states," it added.
Europe's advertising industry sees the case as a critical test of its right to provide services across the EU.
Sweden has argued that children cannot always differ between advertisements and TV programmes. It is the only EU country that has a general ban on advertising aimed at children under 12.

The court had been asked to decide whether EU law allowed Sweden to bar advertisements aired by a TV channel based in a member state where they are legal and also whether the Swedish ban constituted a trade barrier and was therefore contrary to the EU's Treaty of Rome.

The case involved an advertisement for a magazine about dinosaurs that publishing firm De Agostini Forlag AB aired on television channels TV3 and TV4 in 1993. TV3 is a British-based channel broadcasting to Sweden while TV4 is based in Sweden.
Swedish Consumer Ombudsman Axel Edling, saying the advertisement should be banned, decided to take De Agostini to the Swedish Market Court, which asked for a preliminary ruling from the EU court.
"The ruling of the EU court means that Sweden cannot intervene against commercials from other member states," said lawyer Peter Danowsky, who represented De Agostini.
But he added that the Swedish ban on advertising aimed at children in principle continued to be in force for TV4.
"That of course affects the competitive situation between TV3 and TV4," he said in a statement.
Edling said the verdict was a "partial victory," the Swedish news agency TT reported from Stockholm.
The court battle is a sign of the realities of the new television age with authorities unable to control the contents of programmes broadcast from another country.
